prime.problem: If every callback must subclass one concrete base, a class that already is-a Widget gets forced into a family it doesn't belong to. If you declare nothing, the contract lives only in your head and a missing method surfaces in production.
prime.fits: Third OOD card, after inheritance. You've met the abstract base class as the parent of one family; this card sets it beside the interface (a can-do promise any class can sign) and shows Python's two tools for them: abc.ABC and typing.Protocol.
prime.goal: Choose between a Protocol and an ABC for a given design, and predict when Python will refuse to build an object.

attend: ProgressBar never names StatusCallback. Why does isinstance(ProgressBar("p"), StatusCallback) still return True?
In XMLReaderBase, which method is written once for everyone and which does each subclass write?
What does Python's "usually one base" answer look like, compared with Java's extends … implements …?
Why is failing at construction better than a base method that raises NotImplementedError?
What does @runtime_checkable actually check, and what does it miss?

must: Interface = method signatures only → any class with those methods fits (Protocol matches by shape) → unrelated classes can each sign the same can-do contract without sharing a parent
Abstract class = some code written, some left abstract → subclasses inherit the written part (from_string) and fill the core (from_reader) → shared code lives once, for one is-a family
Any unfilled @abstractmethod → the class can't be instantiated → the TypeError names the missing method at construction → bugs surface before any method runs, unlike NotImplementedError
Rule of thumb: code to share among close relatives → ABC; a behaviour any class can have → Protocol; a single-method callback → often just a Callable
elevated: @runtime_checkable checks method names only → a wrong signature still passes isinstance → real Protocol checking happens in a static type checker (mypy), not at run time
reference: the source's C++/Java StatusCallback code and the stray footnote
the full MRO list for MyClass

compress.prompt: Without scrolling, draw the card's diagram: StatusCallback as a dashed interface with ProgressBar fitting it by shape, and XMLReaderBase with one written and one abstract method. Then write the rule of thumb for choosing each in one sentence.
checklist: interface: a promise with no code; Protocol fits by shape
abstract class: partial code; ABC fits by ancestry
neither can be instantiated; a missing abstract method fails at construction
Python allows many bases; MRO orders them
share code → ABC; define a behaviour any class can have → Protocol

retrieve.q: Explain the difference between sharing a promise and sharing code, with StatusCallback and XMLReaderBase as the examples.
answer: StatusCallback promises one method; it carries no code
XMLReaderBase ships from_string once and leaves from_reader to subclasses
promise → any class can fit; code → only subclasses benefit

retrieve.q: Walk through EtreeReader().from_string("<feed><item/><item/></feed>"): which class defines each method that runs, and what comes back?
answer: it wraps the string in io.StringIO and calls self.from_reader
EtreeReader's from_reader parses it: root <feed> with 2 children

retrieve.q: A plain base class raises NotImplementedError; an ABC uses @abstractmethod. When does each one fail if a subclass forgets the method, and why does the card prefer one?
answer: NotImplementedError: the object builds fine and fails at the first call, maybe in production
ABC: fails at construction, with the method named
earlier and louder failure is cheaper to fix

compare.q: Shape was an ABC with no written methods except __init__. Should it have been a Protocol instead? What does each choice give paint_shapes, and what does each lose?
answer: ABC: shared center state, construction-time errors, and isinstance(s, Shape)
Protocol: any class with draw and bounds fits, without subclassing
Protocol loses shared state and construction checks; ABC forces ancestry

compare.q: read4 is a fixed interface you must build on, and the design question is where the leftover buffer lives. How does that relate to this card's split between contract and implementation?
answer: the caller sees one contract: read(n)
the buffer is implementation state behind it, owned by the reader object
an ABC-style base could supply read() once over an abstract read4-like primitive: the XMLReader pattern

predict.q: You write class Quiet: def update_status(self): pass (no old, new parameters). Before running: does isinstance(Quiet(), StatusCallback) return True, and what happens when notify calls it?
predict.answer: It returns True: @runtime_checkable checks only that a method with that name exists. The call cb.update_status(3, 7) then fails with a TypeError about the arguments, at call time. A static checker such as mypy would flag the mismatched signature before you run anything, which is where Protocols are really checked.

apply.task: Build a read-only mapping by subclassing collections.abc.Mapping: a Config that wraps a dict. Write only the 3 abstract methods. Then show that the 6 free methods work (in, keys, items, values, get, ==). Finally, delete __len__ and record exactly when and how it fails.
apply.done: With three methods written, all six free operations work on your Config, and without __len__ the line Config({...}) raises TypeError naming __len__ before any method runs.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: what runtime_checkable accepts?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: nominal (by ancestry) vs structural (by shape) matching?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: abstract method → construction error, or Protocol → no shared parent needed?
In a codebase you know, which base class is really just a promise and should be a Protocol?
What will you look for in the OOD practice card: which relation (is-a, has-a, can-do) each prompt needs?
